lessons.title: Sound recognition: vowel sounds
lessons.objective: Distinguish single vowel sounds (monophthongs), double vowel sounds (diphthongs) and triple vowel sounds (triphthongs) and pronounce them well.
lessons.course:
Some vowel sounds are single: the sound in “sit”, “bed”, “cup”, “food”. Some glide from one sound to another (diphthongs): “day”, “eye”, “boy”, “go”, “cow”. A few glide through three sounds (triphthongs): “fire”, “hour”, “player”.
Good pronunciation helps people understand us, for example at the clinic: “pain”, “cough”, “fever”.
lessons.model: The adult says “bed” (one sound) and “day” (the voice glides). The children feel the difference with a hand under the chin.
lessons.guided: Listen to pairs of words and say whether the vowel sound is single or gliding: bed/day, cup/cow, sit/sight.
lessons.exercise: Is the vowel sound in “boy” single or gliding?
lessons.remediation: Work with three diphthongs only: day, eye, boy.
lessons.transfer: Find three health words with a gliding vowel sound (pain, eye, nose).

practice.prompt: Listen and repeat the words. Which one has a gliding sound?
Which word has a triphthong (three sounds)?
practice.explanation: fire: the voice glides through three sounds.

practice.prompt: Sort: single or gliding?
practice.answer: sit: single; go: gliding; cup: single.

lessons.title: Reading a short story silently: at the health centre
lessons.objective: Read a short story silently and answer literal and inference questions.
lessons.course: Some answers are written in the text (literal questions). Others must be guessed from clues (inference questions): “Why was Enow sad?” We look for clues and explain with “because”.

support.title: Read silently
support.text: Enow woke up with a high fever and a headache. His mother touched his forehead and took him to the health centre. The nurse tested his blood and said, “It is malaria.” She gave him tablets and told him to sleep under a mosquito net every night. After three days, Enow went back to school, but he kept the net over his bed.

lessons.model: The adult reads silently, then says: “The text says he had a fever — that is literal. He kept the net — I guess he did not want to be sick again — that is inference.”
lessons.guided: Read silently. Answer two literal questions and one inference question.
lessons.exercise: What did the nurse say Enow had?
lessons.remediation: Underline the answers in the text before saying them.
lessons.transfer: Read a health leaflet with an adult and say one thing you learnt.

practice.prompt: What two symptoms did Enow have?
practice.answer: A high fever and a headache.
accept: a high fever and a headache
A high fever and a headache
practice.explanation: It is written in the first sentence.

practice.prompt: Why did Enow keep the net over his bed?
choices: so that he would not get malaria again
practice.answer: so that he would not get malaria again
practice.explanation: Inference: the net protects from mosquitoes.

practice.prompt: How many days later did Enow go back to school?
practice.explanation: The text says: After three days.

lessons.title: Dictation: sentences and a short paragraph
lessons.objective: Write dictated sentences and a short paragraph with correct spelling and punctuation.
lessons.course:
During a dictation, we listen to the whole sentence first, then write group of words by group of words. We check capital letters, full stops and difficult words.
Before the dictation, we study the difficult words: healthy, vegetables, every, enough, water.

support.title: Words to study
support.text: healthy  vegetables  every  enough  water  fruit

lessons.model: The adult reads a sentence once, then in groups of words, then once more to check.
lessons.guided: Study the words, then listen to the dictation and write. Check with the text.
lessons.exercise: Spell the word we study: v-e-g-…
lessons.remediation: Do the dictation one sentence at a time, checking after each one.
lessons.transfer: Ask an adult to dictate two sentences to you each day.

practice.prompt: Listen to the dictation and write it.
practice.listen: To stay healthy, we eat fruit and vegetables every day. We drink enough clean water.
practice.answer: To stay healthy, we eat fruit and vegetables every day. We drink enough clean water.
practice.explanation: Check capitals, commas and full stops.

practice.prompt: Which word is spelt correctly?
Put the steps of a dictation in order.

lessons.title: Pronouns: subject, object and possessive
lessons.objective: Use subject, object and possessive pronouns correctly.
lessons.course:
Subject pronouns do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. She helps the nurse.
Object pronouns receive the action: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. The nurse helps her.
Possessive pronouns show who owns: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. This net is mine.
lessons.model: The adult points: “He gives the tablets to her. The tablets are hers now.”
lessons.guided: Replace nouns with pronouns in five sentences about a visit to the clinic.
lessons.exercise: Replace the words: The doctor examined Enow. → The doctor examined ___.
lessons.remediation: Practise subject pronouns, then object pronouns, before possessives.
lessons.transfer: Tell a short story about your family using he, she, him, her.

practice.prompt: Complete with the right pronoun.
practice.text: Mama gave the medicine to [[us]]. [[We]] took it after the meal.
practice.explanation: us is an object; we is a subject.

practice.prompt: Which word is a possessive pronoun?
Match the subject pronoun with its object pronoun.
practice.explanation: Each subject pronoun has an object form.

lessons.title: Proper fractions
lessons.objective: Read, write and represent proper fractions of a whole.
lessons.course:
A fraction is a part of a whole divided into equal parts. In ¾, the denominator (4) is the number of equal parts; the numerator (3) is the number of parts taken.
In a proper fraction, the numerator is smaller than the denominator: ½, ⅓, ¾, ⅖.
lessons.model: The adult cuts a pawpaw into 4 equal parts and takes 3: “three quarters, ¾”.
lessons.guided: Fold paper into 2, 4 and 8 equal parts. Shade parts and write the fraction.
lessons.exercise: A cake is cut into 8 equal pieces. Bih eats 3. What fraction did she eat?
lessons.remediation: Use halves and quarters with real fruit first.
lessons.transfer: Find fractions at home: half a loaf, a quarter of an orange.

practice.prompt: In ⅗, what is the denominator?
practice.explanation: The denominator is the bottom number.

practice.prompt: Which one is a proper fraction?
Shade 3/4 of a rectangle cut into 4 equal parts.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator
lessons.objective: Add and subtract fractions that have the same denominator.
lessons.course:
When the denominators are the same, we add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7; 5/8 − 2/8 = 3/8.
If the result equals the denominator, we have one whole: 3/5 + 2/5 = 5/5 = 1.
lessons.model: A nurse gives 1/4 of a bottle of syrup in the morning and 2/4 in the evening: 3/4 of the bottle.
lessons.guided: Use paper strips divided into eighths to add and subtract fractions.
lessons.remediation: Shade the parts on a strip before calculating.
lessons.transfer: Share a fruit and say what fraction was eaten and what is left.

practice.prompt: Complete.
Manka drinks 2/5 of her water. What fraction is left?

lessons.title: Finite and infinite sets; elements and symbols
lessons.objective: Distinguish finite and infinite sets and use the symbols ∈, ∉ and Ø.
lessons.course:
A finite set has a number of elements we can count: {days of the week} has 7 elements. An infinite set never ends: {1, 2, 3, 4, …}.
∈ means “is an element of”: Monday ∈ {days of the week}. ∉ means “is not an element of”. Ø or { } is the empty set: {children in our class older than 50 years} = Ø.
lessons.guided: Sort sets into finite or infinite. Write three sentences with ∈ and ∉.
lessons.exercise: Is the set of even numbers finite or infinite?
lessons.remediation: Count the elements of small sets to see that they end.
lessons.transfer: Give an example of an empty set in your home.

practice.prompt: Which set is finite?
practice.explanation: There are 12 months: we can count them.

practice.prompt: Complete with ∈ or ∉.
How many elements does the empty set have?
practice.explanation: The empty set has no element.

lessons.title: Ranking data in ascending and descending order
lessons.objective: Rank data in ascending and descending order and read a table.
lessons.course:
Ascending order goes from the smallest to the biggest; descending order from the biggest to the smallest.
A table of data: children vaccinated at the health centre — Monday 34, Tuesday 52, Wednesday 27, Thursday 45. In descending order: 52, 45, 34, 27.
lessons.model: The adult ranks the days from the busiest to the quietest at the health centre.
lessons.guided: Rank the heights or ages of family members in both orders.
lessons.remediation: Compare two numbers at a time.
lessons.transfer: Rank the prices of five things in a shop.

practice.prompt: Put in descending order.
Which day had the fewest vaccinations?
How many more children on Tuesday than on Monday?

lessons.title: Water-borne, insect-borne and air-borne diseases
lessons.objective: Relate symptoms to some common diseases, say how they spread and how to prevent them, including by vaccination.
lessons.course:
Some diseases spread through dirty water or food (cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea), through insects (malaria by mosquitoes), or through the air (tuberculosis, measles, colds).
We prevent them: drink clean water, wash hands, cook food well, sleep under a treated net, cover the mouth when coughing, and get vaccinated. Vaccines protect the body before the disease comes.
lessons.model: The adult reads a child health card: “Vaccinated against measles and polio. Next appointment: …”
lessons.guided: Make a table with three columns (water, insects, air) and place diseases and prevention measures in it.
lessons.answer: Through the bite of a mosquito.
accept: Through the bite of a mosquito
lessons.remediation: Start with one disease for each column.
lessons.transfer: Check your health card with your parents and see which vaccines you received.
lessons.materials: Pictures, a child health card (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Match each disease with how it spreads.
practice.answer: cholera: water; malaria: mosquitoes; tuberculosis: air.

practice.prompt: What does a vaccine do?
choices: protects the body before the disease comes
practice.answer: protects the body before the disease comes
practice.explanation: Vaccines prepare the body to fight a disease.

practice.prompt: Name one way to prevent water-borne diseases.
practice.explanation: Clean water and hygiene prevent them.

lessons.title: J’ai mal à la tête, j’ai froid
lessons.objective: Exprimer une sensation, un sentiment ou une douleur.
lessons.course:
Pour dire une douleur : « J’ai mal à la tête. » « J’ai mal au ventre. » « J’ai mal aux dents. »
Pour dire une sensation : « J’ai froid. » « J’ai chaud. » « J’ai faim. » « J’ai soif. »
Pour dire un sentiment : « Je suis content. » « Je suis triste. » « Je suis fâché. »

support.title: Dis avec l’adulte
support.text:
J’ai mal à la tête.
J’ai soif.
Je suis content.

lessons.model: Chez l’infirmière, Enow dit : « Bonjour, madame. J’ai mal au ventre et j’ai chaud. »
lessons.guided: Jeu de rôle : l’un est l’infirmier, l’autre le malade. Le malade dit où il a mal.
lessons.exercise: Tu veux boire de l’eau. Que dis-tu ?
lessons.remediation: Montre une partie du corps et dis « J’ai mal à… ».
lessons.transfer: Dis en français comment tu te sens ce soir.
lessons.materials: Images de visages et du corps.

practice.prompt: Relie la phrase et sa traduction.
practice.answer: faim : hungry ; froid : cold ; triste : sad.
practice.explanation: Avec faim, soif, froid, chaud, on dit « j’ai ».

practice.prompt: Complète.
practice.text: J’ai mal [[à la]] tête. J’ai mal [[au]] ventre.
practice.explanation: à la + nom féminin ; au + nom masculin.

practice.prompt: Quelle phrase dit un sentiment ?

lessons.title: WHO, UNICEF and WFP: who helps our health?
lessons.objective: Identify some international institutions and their work for children and health.
lessons.course: Some international organisations help countries: WHO (World Health Organization) works for health and vaccination; UNICEF helps children (health, education, protection); WFP (World Food Programme) gives food in hard times; UNESCO works for education and culture. Local NGOs also help communities.
lessons.model: At the health centre, a poster says that the vaccination campaign is supported by WHO and UNICEF.
lessons.guided: Match each organisation with its work. Find a poster or a sign with one of these names in your town.
lessons.exercise: Which organisation works mainly for health?
lessons.remediation: Learn two names first: WHO for health, UNICEF for children.
lessons.transfer: Look for the logo of an organisation on a health card or a poster.
lessons.materials: Posters or pictures (logos described by the adult).

practice.prompt: Match each organisation with its work.
practice.answer: WHO: health; UNICEF: children; WFP: food.

practice.prompt: Which organisation works for education and culture?
practice.explanation: UNESCO works for education, science and culture.

practice.prompt: What does WFP give in hard times?
practice.explanation: WFP is the World Food Programme.

lessons.title: Keeping food and making fruit juice hygienically
lessons.objective: Describe ways of conserving food and prepare a fruit juice hygienically.
lessons.course:
We conserve food so that it lasts longer: drying (maize, fish), smoking (fish, meat), frying, keeping cool. Spoiled food can make us sick.
To make a juice: wash hands, wash the fruits, use clean tools, squeeze or blend, add clean water, cover and drink it quickly.
lessons.model: The adult prepares orange juice: washes hands and oranges, squeezes them into a clean jug and covers it.
lessons.guided: Prepare a fruit juice with the adult following the hygiene rules. Name one food your family dries or smokes.
lessons.exercise: Name one way to conserve fish.
lessons.remediation: Learn two ways of conserving food first: drying and smoking.
lessons.transfer: Make a juice for your family and explain the hygiene rules.
lessons.materials: Fruits, a clean jug, a squeezer, clean water.

practice.prompt: Put the steps of making a juice in order.
Which food is often dried in the sun?
practice.explanation: Maize is dried to keep it.

practice.prompt: Why must we conserve food well?
practice.answer: So that it does not spoil and make us sick.

lessons.title: Traditional and modern dance steps
lessons.objective: Identify dance steps, dance following a rhythm and appreciate the dances of different peoples.
lessons.course:
Each people has traditional dances for ceremonies (birth, harvest, enthronement) with costumes and instruments. Modern dances are danced at parties and on radio or TV music.
To dance well: listen to the rhythm, start with simple steps (step-together, side-to-side), then add arm movements. We respect the meaning of traditional dances.
lessons.model: The adult shows a step-together to the right and to the left, following a drum beat.
lessons.guided: Learn four steps following a drum. Ask an elder about one traditional dance of your area and when it is danced.
lessons.exercise: When are traditional dances often danced?
lessons.remediation: Clap the rhythm before moving the feet.
lessons.transfer: Dance the steps with your family at home.
lessons.materials: A drum or recorded music, open space.

practice.prompt: Put the dance steps in order.
practice.answer: right, bring left, left, bring right.

practice.prompt: What do we listen to before dancing?
Name a ceremony with traditional dance in your area.
practice.answer: For example: a harvest festival or an enthronement.

lessons.title: Hopscotch and galloping games
lessons.objective: Hop, gallop and play hopscotch following the rules.
lessons.course:
Hopscotch: draw squares numbered 1 to 8 on the ground. Throw a stone into square 1, hop over it on one foot, go to the end and come back, pick up the stone without putting the other foot down.
Galloping: one foot leads, the other follows, like a horse.
lessons.model: The adult draws the hopscotch and plays one turn while counting the squares.
lessons.guided: Draw a hopscotch and play with friends, taking turns. Gallop around a circle.
lessons.exercise: On how many feet do we hop?
lessons.remediation: Hop on one foot five times before playing.
lessons.transfer: Teach the hopscotch game to a younger child.
lessons.materials: Chalk or a stick, a flat stone.

practice.prompt: The stone is in square 5. How many squares before it?
Draw a hopscotch with eight numbered squares.
What do we do when it is not our turn?

lessons.title: Telling a folktale
lessons.objective: Listen to and retell a short folktale and draw its lesson.
lessons.course:
Folktales are old stories told by elders, often at night. Animals talk and act like people. Each tale has a lesson.
To tell a tale: begin with a traditional opening, tell the events in order, use your voice and gestures, end with the lesson.

support.title: A short original tale
support.text: Tortoise wanted all the groundnuts of the village. At night, he took them and hid them in his shell. But the shell was too full, and he could not walk. In the morning, the villagers found him on the road. Tortoise was ashamed and gave back the groundnuts.

lessons.model: The adult tells the tale with a big voice for Tortoise and a sad voice at the end.
lessons.guided: Retell the tale in your own words. Then ask an elder for a tale in the family language and retell it.
lessons.exercise: What is the lesson of the tale?
lessons.remediation: Retell the tale with three pictures: taking, hiding, being found.
lessons.transfer: Ask an elder for a tale of your people and tell it to a friend.

practice.prompt: Put the events of the tale in order.
items: He hid them in his shell.
practice.answer: took, hid, could not walk, gave back.

practice.prompt: Why could Tortoise not walk?
Listen to the tale.
practice.listen: Tortoise wanted all the groundnuts of the village. At night, he took them and hid them in his shell. But the shell was too full, and he could not walk. In the morning, the villagers found him on the road. Tortoise was ashamed and gave back the groundnuts.
practice.explanation: Retell it in your own words.

lessons.title: Using the mouse: click, double-click, drag
lessons.objective: Describe the functions of the mouse and select and drag objects on the desktop.
lessons.course:
The mouse moves the pointer on the screen. Click (left button once) selects. Double-click opens. Right-click shows a menu. Drag: hold the left button, move, release.
The Start menu (bottom of the screen) opens programs; the desktop shows icons.
lessons.model: The adult clicks the Start menu, double-clicks an icon to open it, then drags a file icon to a new place.
lessons.guided: With an adult, open the Start menu, open Notepad with a double-click, then drag an icon on the desktop.
lessons.answer: It opens a program or a file.
accept: It opens a program or a file
lessons.remediation: Practise clicking on large icons first.
lessons.transfer: Show an adult how to drag an icon.
lessons.materials: A computer with a mouse (with an adult).

practice.prompt: Match each action with its result.
practice.answer: click: select; double-click: open; right-click: menu.

practice.prompt: Put the drag in order.
Where is the Start menu usually?
choices: at the bottom of the screen
practice.answer: at the bottom of the screen
